title: Both steps went downhill. Only one passed the line.
usage: Reviewed exam-eve walkthrough content. Plain-text explanations only; the concept sketch is hand-authored SVG, described below. Scenario choices are page state and never modify coverage, pins, priority, or exported notebook data.

scenarios.heading: Scenario A · Reading the rule
scenarios.setup: You are line searching along a downhill direction. Two candidate steps both lower the objective, one small and one large. Armijo compares the actual decrease against the slope-predicted decrease, the straight sufficient-decrease line through the current value with slope c1 times the directional derivative.

choices.label: Any decrease passes
choices.reveal: A drop by itself is not the test. Armijo asks for a decrease proportional to the step length and the local slope, so a long step that barely lowers the value can fail while going downhill.

choices.label: The largest step passes
choices.reveal: The large step did lower the value, but not by enough for its length, so it sits above the sufficient-decrease line. The line, not the curve, is the test, and a longer step owes a larger predicted decrease.

choices.label: Only the point below the sufficient-decrease line passes
choices.reveal: Armijo accepts exactly the steps whose actual decrease reaches the slope-predicted decrease. The smaller step lands below the line, so its drop beats the prediction and it passes.

visual.label: Concept sketch
visual.description: A hand-authored, qualitative plot of objective value against step size along the search direction. The curve leaves the current value, dips, and climbs again, while the straight sufficient-decrease line leaves the same point with slope c1 times the directional derivative. A dashed candidate labelled "Large step, fails" sits on the curve above the line, and a solid candidate labelled "Small step, passes" sits on the curve below it. Diagram labels stay readable as text on mobile; dashed versus solid lines carry the distinction as well as colour.
visual.screenReaderSummary: Concept sketch: plotted against step size, the large candidate sits above the sufficient-decrease line and fails, while the small candidate sits below the line and passes.

scenarios.heading: Scenario B · Why not tiny steps?
scenarios.setup: Your solver keeps shrinking the candidate step. Every tiny step passes Armijo, yet the objective barely moves and you are stuck far from the minimum.
scenarios.prompt: Why is Armijo alone not enough?

choices.label: It accepts steps that are too small, so you stall.
choices.reveal: A tiny step almost always clears the sufficient-decrease line, so Armijo accepts it while progress crawls. The curvature condition, the second Wolfe condition, is what rules out steps that are too small.

choices.label: It always rejects steps.
choices.reveal: The setup says every tiny step passes, so rejection is not what is happening. The trouble is the opposite: Armijo accepts too easily at the small end and never asks whether the step made meaningful progress.

scenarios.takeaway: Armijo alone can bless uselessly tiny steps, and the curvature condition completes the test by demanding that the directional slope has actually flattened.
